children: The Australian dollar, often seen as a proxy for global investor sentiment, rallied more than 5% against the U.S. dollar from the end of June until early this month, but has come under pressure lately and technical analysis suggests further declines could be ahead.
Click here for a more detailed chart.

The weakness in the Australian dollar — or aussie — in recent days has been fueled by a surging U.S. dollar, rising U.S. Treasury yields, and global risk aversion tied to energy and inflation concerns. The technical picture has also begun to work against the Australian dollar, with several bearish signals indicating that the uptrend could be in trouble.

The first reversal signal came on September 10, when the aussie closed below its 10-day moving average. A similar signal followed on September 14, with the currency tumbling below its 20-day moving average — both lending weight to the trend reversal argument. Technical analysts use moving averages to strip out price extremes to gain a clearer picture of market direction.

Adding to the bearish case is a twist in what is known as the Ichimoku cloud. An Ichimoku cloud is a system of calculations similar to moving averages used to gauge price trends. A twist in this cloud is a forward-projected indicator that signals a shift in market balance before price fully reacts.

The upcoming twist appears on the daily chart on September 17, with parameters of 0.7020-0.7024, according to data supplied by LSEG. Such twists only carry significance when they coincide with a peak or trough in the market, such as the nearly four-month high of 0.7238 hit on September 9.
Targets for further losses would include the 100-day moving average at 0.7080 and the 200-day average at 0.7000. Below there could facilitate a slide back to the June 30 low of 0.6867.
However, the developing bearish structure would be negated should it close back above the 10-day moving average at 0.7180.
Uptrend halted after peaking at 0.7238 on September 9
